opinions.rationale: Inverted prior: treat missing-eligibility selection as already handled, then check what exists. Three direct method papers (not one) address the complete-case selection problem under explicit missingness models. Tompsett et al. (2023) formalize bias from missing eligibility in a point-treatment TTE, show patterns under MAR and MNAR, and evaluate multiple imputation of the eligibility-defining variables plus MNAR sensitivity shifts; they state that MNAR imputation remains exploratory because the sensitivity parameters are not identified from the data alone. Benz et al. (2025; also arXiv:2406.16830), which the entry cites as the first direct treatment, develops inverse-probability-of-ascertainment weights for sequential TTE with time-to-event endpoints under an eligibility-MAR assumption (ascertainment independent of true eligibility given non-eligibility covariates and treatment), evaluates them in plasmode EHR simulations, and applies them to a Kaiser Permanente bariatric-surgery cohort; accompanying research code is on GitHub (lbenz730/missing_eligibility_tte), not a production CRAN/Python package. Shen et al. (2026, Stat Med) compares complete-case analysis with three multiple-imputation strategies for eligibility-defining variables in EHR survival TTEs and reports that flexible MI often reduces bias when missingness is high. Wang et al. (2026) map eligibility realization in EHR data and cite Tompsett and Benz as the handling literature; they do not add a new estimator. What remains open, and matches the entry’s harder claim, is latent eligibility: an absent lab is consistent with never-tested versus would-have-failed, with recording driven by the same severity that predicts treatment and outcome (MNAR not cured by MAR IPW or standard MI). No paper retrieved jointly models true eligibility and its observation process anchored to a validation source where the criterion was assessed for everyone; no head-to-head of MI, IPW, doubly robust selection correction, and partial-identification bounds on the same TTE data with reporting of the implied eligible population under each method was found. Package search (TrialEmulation, WeightIt missing-covariate handling, gfoRmula, lmtp, ltmle, zEpid, causallib) shows no shipped inverse-probability-of-eligibility-ascertainment or joint latent-eligibility measurement model. 2025–2026 guidance (TARGET, FDA RWE/ECT, EMA registry, NICE RWE) does not resolve identification of latent eligibility. Partial solve covers MAR complete-case selection; the title problem (unrecorded criterion indistinguishable from met criterion) stays open.

opinions.rationale: Inverted prior: treat collider-inducing eligibility as already audited in routine TTE workflows, then search for a method or tool that does so. Found conceptual and design literature, not a solution. Hernán and Robins (2016) already require that eligibility not use postbaseline events; that is design discipline, not an automated check of whether a healthcare-use criterion is a collider. Weiskopf et al. (2023, JAMIA) explicitly frame healthcare utilization as a common collider in EHR reuse and warn that conditioning on utilization (by selection or adjustment) opens non-causal paths; Digitale et al. (2023, J Clin Epidemiol) likewise describe collider-conditioning bias when restricting to people in care or with a disease history. Wang et al. (2026) restate that conditioning eligibility on utilization induces collider bias at cohort entry. These works strengthen that the mechanism is real; they do not supply a certified check. TARGET (Hansford et al., 2025) requires reporting of eligibility criteria and their emulation, not assessment of the selection graph those criteria induce; the entry’s reading of TARGET is accurate. Practical reviews (e.g., Tran et al., 2026) continue to document post-treatment eligibility as a frequent high-risk design error, which is evidence the gap is still live in applications. No retrieved paper or package implements a causal-discovery or temporal-rule eligibility auditor for proposed TTE criteria with evaluation on known graphs (sensitivity, false-positive rate, expert agreement, bias reduction when acting on warnings). Federated causal discovery and general DAG tools exist in adjacent literature but are not integrated into TTE protocol design or reporting checklists. Graph learning recovering only a Markov equivalence class under latent confounding remains a structural limit, as the entry states; formalizations of that limit do not close the problem. Queries run: collider + eligibility + target trial (2024–2026); healthcare utilization collider + eligibility; TARGET checklist collider/selection; causal discovery eligibility auditor TTE; CRAN/GitHub TrialEmulation, WeightIt, MatchIt, cobalt for eligibility-collider features (none found). Open as a workflow and tooling problem; prior art names the bias and forbids postbaseline criteria but does not solve systematic detection of healthcare-use colliders in eligibility definitions.
